source.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
source.authors: Jacob Dunefsky; Philippe Chlenski; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates learned feature dictionaries in GPT2-small and Pythia models, providing LLM-setting evidence relevant to V4; it does not reproduce the toy-model superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition as motivation but does not test superposition geometry, feature sparsity or importance transitions, or feature competition for capacity. Its SAE comparison and human-rated feature results bear on V4. The circuit case studies use transcoders rather than SAEs and do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper builds and evaluates transcoders as a circuit-analysis tool. SAEs appear only as the comparison baseline for sparsity, fidelity and interpretability. It never asks whether LLM features are superposed, how many neurons features span, or whether dictionaries recover the model's units. It cites superposition only as the motivation for SAEs. The SAE numbers are a method baseline, not a test of V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that transcoders match or beat SAEs on sparsity, faithfulness and human-rated interpretability. They say transcoders enable input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs, and they consider transcoders an improvement over MLP-output SAEs. They acknowledge that transcoders are lossy approximations, that attention patterns are treated as fixed, and that the circuit evidence rests on a few qualitative case studies.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains wide sparse MLP transcoders to approximate MLP input-output behavior and compares them with SAEs; it does not use the original toy-model setup or its feature-geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that results depend on the sparsity coefficient λ1 and acknowledge that the learning rate may not be optimal for SAEs; compute limitations prevented exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps.

fits_no_version.finding: In a blinded single-rater check of 50 random Pythia-410M layer-15 features, 38 of 50 MLP-in SAE features and 41 of 50 transcoder features were judged interpretable. Transcoders matched or beat SAEs on sparsity-loss frontiers across GPT2-small, Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transcoders (sparse MLP replacements) yield features at least as interpretable and faithful as SAEs. This is a dictionary-method comparison, not evidence about superposition itself.

record.problems: The authors note that transcoders are approximations whose errors may lose key information; their circuit method treats attention patterns as fixed; circuit evidence is based on a few qualitative case studies; and compute limits prevented exhaustive SAE/transcoder hyperparameter sweeps. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the feature-rating counts.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for individual points in Figure 3: the plots show multiple λ1 settings, but the text reports the comparison at the frontier level and the individual plotted values are not stated numerically. Transcoder circuit case studies in §§5 and H are not SAE results and do not test the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No toy models, geometry or sparsity-dependent transition.
No test of capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
No measurement of features spread across neurons. SAE interpretability is reported only as a baseline for the tool comparison.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicality of SAE features. Comparing transcoder and SAE features is left to future work.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with V4 supports/limits_scope labels is overturned. The SAE data are baselines for the paper's own tool, and r3/r4 are pair-selection values. A limits_scope label based on the transcoder outperforming the SAE would misread a method comparison as a test of the claim. Interpretability counts come from one rater with no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network experiment, superposition geometry measurement, or sparsity-dependent transition is tested.
The paper mentions neuron polysemanticity but does not test whether capacity competition causes it or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
No alternative cause of polysemantic neurons is tested.

The paper rates a sample of SAE features for interpretability and evaluates sparsity and fidelity, but does not measure how many neurons each underlying feature spans or establish that the recovered features exhaustively capture model representations.
Feature completeness, stability across training runs or settings, and canonicality are not tested.
The paper does not test whether the model's underlying features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional structures.

rows.subject: Pythia-410M layer 15 SAE
rows.operation_detail: A human rater assessed 50 randomly selected features in a blinded comparison.

conditions.value: blinded human assessment using top-activating examples

rows.note: The paper reports aggregate counts for the 50 sampled features.
rows.check: The SAE is a baseline in a method comparison (Table 1). One rater judged 50 features without uncertainty, framed as transcoder vs SAE, not as evidence that LLMs hold dictionary-recoverable sparse features. At most it is weak indirect context for V4, not a test of it.

rows.subject: Pythia-410M layer 15 transcoder
rows.operation_detail: A human rater assessed 50 randomly selected features in a blinded comparison.

conditions.value: blinded human assessment using top-activating examples

rows.baseline: Pythia-410M layer 15 SAE: 38 interpretable, 8 maybe interpretable, 4 uninterpretable
rows.note: The paper reports aggregate counts for the 50 sampled features. The transcoder is a comparator, not an SAE.
rows.check: This is the study's own method (transcoder) compared with the SAE. It is a tool-performance result, not a measurement of superposition.

rows.subject: Pythia-410M layer 15 SAE
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated mean activation sparsity and model loss after replacing the MLP with the learned dictionary.

conditions.value: SAE trained on MLP inputs with λ1 = 7.0 × 10−5

rows.baseline: Pythia-410M layer 15 transcoder: mean L0 44.04 and cross-entropy 3.35 nats
rows.note: The paper says this SAE/transcoder pair was selected because their sparsity–cross-entropy performance was similar.
rows.check: These are selection values. Appendix F reports them to justify choosing this SAE/transcoder pair for the interpretability comparison. They are not a result on any version.

rows.subject: Pythia-410M layer 15 transcoder
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated mean activation sparsity and model loss after replacing the MLP with the learned dictionary.
rows.baseline: Pythia-410M layer 15 SAE: mean L0 47.85 and cross-entropy 3.36 nats
rows.note: The paper reports this pair as occupying very similar points on the L0–cross-entropy Pareto frontier.
rows.check: These are selection values for the chosen transcoder (Appendix F), and the transcoder is the paper's own method. Not a result on any version.

rows.subject: GPT2-small layer 8 SAE and transcoder
rows.operation_detail: Compared sparsity–accuracy Pareto frontiers for trained SAEs and transcoders.
rows.value: The text reports that transcoders were equal to or better than SAEs in all tested cases.
rows.note: The textual result is a comparison of frontier performance, not a direct measure of SAE feature completeness or interpretability.
rows.check: This is a method comparison of Pareto frontiers (Figure 3), and no numeric values are stated. It measures tool fidelity and sparsity, not superposition.

rows.subject: Pythia-410M layer 15 SAE and transcoder
rows.operation_detail: Compared sparsity–accuracy Pareto frontiers for trained SAEs and transcoders.
rows.value: The text reports that transcoders were equal to or better than SAEs in all tested cases.
rows.note: The paper notes that a more exhaustive hyperparameter sweep could potentially let SAEs surpass transcoders.
rows.check: Same as r5: a method-comparison frontier for Pythia-410M with no superposition measure.

rows.subject: Pythia-1.4B layer 15 SAE and transcoder
rows.operation_detail: Compared sparsity–accuracy Pareto frontiers for trained SAEs and transcoders.
rows.value: The text reports that transcoders were equal to or better than SAEs in all tested cases; the gap appeared to widen on larger models.
rows.note: The authors caution that compute limitations prevented exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps.
rows.check: Same as r5: a method-comparison frontier for Pythia-1.4B. The widening gap concerns transcoders vs SAEs, not superposition.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
